parts.visual:
An oil company spends $50 Million on a marketing campaign showing a single windmill in a green field, while spending $5 Billion drilling for oil in the ocean.

The Tactics:
1. Sustainability: A genuine effort to reduce carbon emissions and environmental impact.
2. ESG Investing: Wall Street funds that refuse to invest in 'dirty' companies.
3. Greenwashing: A deceptive marketing spin used to persuade the public that an organization's products and policies are environmentally friendly, when they actually are not.
parts.audio: Because modern consumers and investors demand environmental responsibility, corporations face immense pressure. This leads to Greenwashing—spending more time and money marketing yourself as 'green' than actually minimizing your environmental impact.

questions.question: A massive fast-fashion brand replaces plastic bags with paper bags in their stores, and launches a massive PR campaign about saving the earth. However, their clothes are still made in sweatshops and create millions of tons of landfill waste. What is this?
options: Textbook Greenwashing. They made a tiny, highly visible change to distract the public from the massive, systemic environmental damage of their core business model.
questions.correct_answer: Textbook Greenwashing. They made a tiny, highly visible change to distract the public from the massive, systemic environmental damage of their core business model.
questions.explanation: Greenwashing relies on the 'Halo Effect'—doing one good thing to mask a hundred bad things.

questions.question: Listen to the CFO. Why is she suddenly interested in 'Carbon Neutrality'?
questions.tts_text: I don't care about the trees. But BlackRock just announced they will pull billions of dollars out of our stock if we don't hit ESG compliance by next year. We have to buy carbon offsets right now.
options: Capital Market Pressure. The biggest investment funds in the world (ESG funds) are using their massive financial power to force companies to comply with environmental standards.
questions.correct_answer: Capital Market Pressure. The biggest investment funds in the world (ESG funds) are using their massive financial power to force companies to comply with environmental standards.
questions.explanation: Corporations change behavior when the cost of capital changes, not when moral arguments are made.

questions.question: What is a 'Carbon Offset'?
options: A certificate a company buys representing the reduction of one metric ton of carbon dioxide. It allows a polluting airline to claim they are 'Carbon Neutral' by paying someone else to plant trees.
questions.correct_answer: A certificate a company buys representing the reduction of one metric ton of carbon dioxide. It allows a polluting airline to claim they are 'Carbon Neutral' by paying someone else to plant trees.
questions.explanation: Carbon offsets are highly controversial, as critics argue they are simply a 'License to Pollute' for the rich.

questions.question: What is 'Scope 3' in corporate emissions reporting?
options: The third floor of the building.
The hardest metric: It requires a company to measure and report not just their own pollution, but the pollution caused by their suppliers *and* the customers using their products.
questions.correct_answer: The hardest metric: It requires a company to measure and report not just their own pollution, but the pollution caused by their suppliers *and* the customers using their products.
questions.explanation: Apple's 'Scope 3' emissions include the electricity you use to charge your iPhone at your house. Forcing companies to report this is a massive regulatory battle.

questions.explanation: The dark art of modern corporate marketing.
